findings.claim: The new `jsonContentTypeRegex` only accepts `application/...` media types, so JSON responses served as `text/json`, `text/x-json`, or any `text/...+json` subtype will no longer be pretty-printed.
findings.rationale: The regex is anchored with `^application\/`. If the previous implementation used a looser check (e.g. `includes('application/json')` or a check that also tolerated other types), this is a silent behavior change for callers that set a non-`application` JSON content type. Medium confidence, since the call site isn't shown in the hunk, but the anchor is clearly restrictive.

findings.claim: The trailing lookahead `(?=$|[;\s])` rejects a comma, so a combined/duplicated header value such as `application/json,application/json` (which fetch/Headers produces when the header is appended twice) will not be recognized as JSON.
findings.rationale: `Headers.get()` joins repeated header values with `, `. With `application/json, application/json` the first value ends with `,`, which is neither end-of-string, `;`, nor whitespace, so the match fails and prettification is skipped. Low-to-medium likelihood in practice but a real edge case; adding `,` to the lookahead character class would cover it.

findings.claim: The structured-suffix subtype pattern `[a-z0-9._-]+\+` does not allow `+` inside the subtype prefix, so media types with more than one suffix segment (e.g. `application/vnd.foo+xml+json`) or subtypes containing other token characters permitted by RFC 6838 (`!#$&^`, etc.) are not matched.
findings.rationale: RFC 6838 restricted-name characters are broader than `[a-z0-9._-]`. This is a narrow edge case and unlikely to matter for real-world APIs, but it means some legitimately JSON-suffixed types are skipped. Low confidence that it matters in practice.

findings.claim: The regex does not tolerate leading whitespace in the header value (e.g. `" application/json"`), since it is anchored at `^`.
findings.rationale: Header values are normally trimmed by the HTTP stack/Headers implementation, so this is mostly theoretical, but if the value is set manually via `c.header('Content-Type', ' application/json')` the check silently fails. Low confidence this is reachable.
